title: Rightly understood, the Reformed doctrine agrees in substance with the more received Thomists
source_text: XXIX. Ex omnibus autem hisce manifestum est Reformatorum hac in parte doctrinam recte expositam atque intellectam, & ex mente eorum a quibus proponitur, reipsa non differre a sententia eorum qui in Schola Romana receptiores Thomistae appellantur. Quamvis enim contendant libertatem opponi non coactioni solum, sed necessitati quoque naturali & proprie dictae, nihilominus agnoscunt positis omnibus quae sunt ad agendum praerequisita, necessario sequi actum creaturae liberae necessitate quadam infallibilitatis. Quia licet agens liberum semper in se retineat potestatem non agendi, etiam quum reipsa agit, & a fortiori quum est in proximo ad agendum; positis tamen omnibus quae, tum ex parte Dei, tum ex parte intellectus praerequiruntur ut voluntas agat, agit illa certo & infallibiliter, & impossibile est actionem ejus non sequi. Nempe ex eorum doctrina, cum omnibus illis quae sunt ad agendum praerequisita optime conjungi & consistere potest potentia non agendi, aut aliter agendi, non tamen carentia actus, & multo minus actus contrarius.
pass_a_gloss: But from all these it is manifest that the doctrine of the Reformed in this part, rightly set forth and understood, and according to the mind of those by whom it is propounded, does not in fact differ from the opinion of those who in the Roman School are called the more received Thomists. For although they contend that liberty is opposed not to compulsion only, but to natural necessity also and necessity properly so called, nevertheless they acknowledge that, all things being posited which are prerequisite to acting, the act of the free creature necessarily follows by a certain necessity of infallibility. Because although a free agent always retains in itself the power of not acting, even when it actually acts, and a fortiori when it is proximate to acting; yet all things being posited which, both on the part of God, and on the part of the intellect, are prerequired that the will may act, it acts certainly and infallibly, and it is impossible that its action not follow. Namely from their doctrine, with all those things which are prerequisite to acting the potency of not acting, or of acting otherwise, can very well be joined and consist, yet not the lack of the act, and much less the contrary act.
pass_b_english: From all this it is clear that the Reformed teaching on this point, correctly stated and understood as its own exponents intend it, does not in fact differ from the view of those in the Roman School called the more widely received Thomists.

These Thomists maintain that freedom is opposed not only to compulsion but also to natural necessity, necessity in the proper sense. Even so, they recognize that once everything required for acting is in place, the free creature's act follows necessarily, with a necessity of infallibility.

A free agent always keeps in itself the power not to act, even while it is actually acting, and all the more when it is on the point of acting. But once everything required on God's side and on the intellect's side for the will to act is in place, the will acts surely and infallibly, and its action cannot fail to follow. On their teaching, then, the power not to act or to act otherwise can perfectly well coexist with everything required for acting, but the absence of the act cannot, and still less a contrary act.

choices.why: Kept as the technical phrase both Reformed parties use; it marks the necessity that removes the power to act otherwise, as against a necessity of infallibility.
